michigan.headline: Michigan Football players, coaches react to offensive coordinator Jason Beck’s firing
michigan.body:
PISCATAWAY, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 31: Wide receiver JJ Buchanan #6 of the Michigan Wolverines looks on during the first quarter against the Rutgers Scarlet Knights at SHI Stadium on October 31, 2026 in Piscataway, New Jersey. (Photo by Mark Smith/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) | ISI Photos via Getty Images

Michigan Wolverines head coach Kyle Whittingham decided to fire offensive coordinator Jason Beck over the weekend. In the aftermath of Beck’s departure, multiple Michigan coaches and players reacted to the offensive coordinator’s firing.

The decision to fire Beck came following an abysmal offensive showing in a 15-6 loss to the Michigan State Spartans. Beck’s offense had significantly underperformed throughout the season and the loss to Michigan State was the final straw.

“Players were disappointed in the game, obviously,” Whittingham said. “They’re a very prideful and competitive group, and so I wouldn’t say anybody is hanging their head or sulking, but they’re all very disappointed and embarrassed by it.”

It was certainly an embarrassing loss as Michigan’s offense continued to sputter, posting 192 yards and just six points. Despite the offensive struggles, losing a coach midseason can be difficult for the program, but it’s a part of the business.

“It’s definitely shocking. It’s a big change in the building,” Buchanan told the media. “He’s one of the reasons that I’m here today so it’s unfortunate, but it’s just the nature of the business. Coach Beck is a great mentor and a great person.”

Buchanan spent his freshman season under Whittingham and Beck at Utah in 2025, so following his head coach and offensive coordinator to Michigan was one of the reasons he transferred. Now less than a year later, Beck has been fired.

“My message to the team has been everybody has to stay together and finish the season out strong,” Buchanan said. “It starts with me being one of the leaders on the team. I have to execute better and that trickles down to everyone else.”

In addition to the players facing a challenging transition following Beck’s firing, the same can be said for the coaches. The impact of a coach being fired can be felt across the coaching staff, in terms of on-field duties and off-field relationships.

“It was tough because he’s a good friend of mine,” defensive ends coach Lewis Powell said. “He’s an awesome coach, and is a great father and husband, but that’s part of the business. He understands that and he’s going to bounce back.”

“It’s very challenging. He’s a good man and a good dad,” special teams coordinator Kerry Coombs said to the media. “My friends are in this building, the players and coaches, so it’s hard. I’m not going to tell you it’s easy because it’s not.”

There’s no doubt that Beck was deservedly fired due to the offensive struggles, but the firing of a coach midseason can often galvanize a program or lead to a further division, so we’ll see how his exit affects the Wolverines moving forward.

michigan.headline: Dan Lanning roasts Michigan HC Kyle Whittingham’s Oregon can ‘outbid everybody’ comments
michigan.body:
Oct 28, 2023; Salt Lake City, Utah, USA; Oregon Ducks head coach Dan Lanning speaks with Utah Utes head coach Kyle Whittingham before a game at Rice-Eccles Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Christopher Creveling-USA TODAY Sports | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con

Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham seems to say something head-scratching nearly every time he’s in front of a microphone. And that happened again earlier this week on the “Inside Michigan Football” radio show.

Here’s a look at Whittingham saying that Oregon can “outbid everybody” in recruiting and what Oregon head coach Dan Lanning said in response.

Whittingham’s quote:

“He really does a great job recruiting. It doesn’t hurt that you have $50 million at your disposal to, in essence, to outbid everybody. Not everybody, but a lot of people. But that’s not his fault. That’s a credit. I mean, that’s a credit to their program and their dedication and desire to win and the support they have. NIL is really the name in the game in recruiting these days; it’s shifted so much. Used to be the facilities you had, the tradition and all these other things; now it’s these guys got 100 grand more for me. It’s a little bit of a factor, to say the least, but not to take anything away from Dan because he’s an outstanding recruiter just in and of itself.”

Lanning’s response:

“I’ve got nothing to say to Coach Whit other than I think he’s an unbelievable coach, and I get it. They’re spending more of their money right now on their coaches that they’re letting go, so maybe it makes it hard to sign players. But I know they’ve signed a couple of guys that we weren’t able to compete with what they decided to do, and maybe a lot of that money is tied up for them in another player. I don’t know. But Coach Whittingham is an unbelievable coach. He’s a Hall of Fame coach. I’ve got nothing but respect for him.”

Dan Lanning’s response to Michigan coach Kyle Whittingham’s comments on Oregon being able to “outbid everybody” for recruits. pic.twitter.com/zsVwvrppUc
— Ryan Clarke (@RyanTClarke) November 11, 2026

Lanning is clearly referring to the roughly $10 million Michigan will still have to pay to former offensive coordinator Jason Beck, who was fired on Sunday. He’s also likely referring to the major NIL deal Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood signed.

Lanning’s comments balance the respect he has for Whittingham as a coach and the reality of Whittingham’s comments being out of touch and senseless. What good did Whittingham do for the Michigan program by saying what he said? If anything, Whittingham gave Oregon bulletin-board material. At 66 years of age, one would think Whittingham would realize what benefits his team and what doesn’t, but here we are. Another wrinkle in Whittingham’s comments is acting like tradition now means less because money is involved — that’s ridiculous — trophy games will always matter; playing Ohio State will always matter, whether he likes it or not.

It’s hard to find any fault in Lanning’s response — he’s not wrong.

michigan.headline: Michigan Football edge rusher Nate Marshall ‘being held accountable’ amid suspension
michigan.body:
PISCATAWAY, NJ - OCTOBER 31: Nate Marshall #94 of the Michigan Wolverines during the game against the Rutgers Scarlet Knights at SHI Stadium on October 31, 2026 in Piscataway, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

After initially being reported that he was no longer part of the program, it was determined that Michigan Wolverines edge rusher Nate Marshall was suspended indefinitely from the team due to undisclosed disciplinary reasons.

During a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, defensive ends coach Lewis Powell spoke about Marshall’s situation.

“I absolutely love Nate. He’s an awesome kid and is a big time talent, but right now he’s been suspended indefinitely,” Powell said. “I’m not sure if he’s going to come back or not yet, but hopefully it all works out.”

There haven’t been any details about the reasoning for Marshall’s indefinite suspension or what led to the decision by the coaching staff, but Powell did say that Marshall is being “held accountable” for his actions.

“We have team rules that we all have to abide by, and he knows what they are, and so he’s being held accountable for that right now,” Powell said. “Later on in life, I think he’ll call me and thank me for what we’re doing right now.”

The initial report about Marshall leaving the program before the clarification certainly makes the situation a bit murkier. It’s also not the first time he has received disciplinary action.

Prior to this season, Marshall was in trouble with the coaching staff for missing classes, per head coach Kyle Whittingham. Whittingham previously spoke to the media about Marshall’s maturity, saying he came a long way since they first met.

“I’m so proud of Nate and how far he’s come since I met him,” Whittingham said in September. “Not only on the field but off the field. He’s making good decisions. He’s going to class. To see him have success on the field is icing on the cake.”

Less than two months later, Whittingham suspended Marshall again, and his time with the program could be coming to an end. He totaled 11 tackles and two sacks in nine games this year.

Marshall’s suspension comes at a very turbulent time in the program. The Wolverines were embarrassed, 15-6, against Michigan State last weekend, resulting in the firing of offensive coordinator Jason Beck.

With just three games left in the season, it remains to be seen if Marshall ever takes another snap at Michigan.

michigan.headline: 1 Fact, 1 Fiction: Michigan Football vs Oregon
michigan.body:
Michigan defensive coordinator Jay Hill waves at fans as the team arrives ahead of the game between Michigan and Penn State at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

There’s been some change in Ann Arbor since Saturday morning. For starters, the Paul Bunyan Trophy now resides in East Lansing for the next year after Michigan State handed Michigan its first loss in the rivalry since 2021. Then, offensive coordinator Jason Beck was fired on Sunday.

Now, Michigan is expected to head to Eugene to take on a team that just dismantled Ohio State on the road. Here is one fact and one fiction heading into Saturday’s matchup between Michigan and Oregon.

Fact: On the bright side, Michigan’s defense is still elite

Amid the firing of Beck and an offense that is one of the worst statistically in Michigan history, the defense is getting overlooked for just how impressive it really is.

When comparing it to some of the great defenses of Michigan’s past decade — 2016, 2018, 2021, 2023 — out of those five years, Michigan is third in points per game (16.2, 14th in NCAA), second in total yards per game (255.3, fourth in NCAA, while 2016 and 2023 Michigan was first in NCAA), third in passing yards (154.8, 4th in NCAA, better than 157 in 2023), and second in rushing yards per game (100.6, 18th in NCAA, only behind 90 yards in 2023). That is insane production considering the Wolverines are 5-4 and have faced three ranked teams, and three more to finish the season.

Against Michigan State, although it didn’t produce any turnovers, the Michigan defense didn’t allow a touchdown and kept the Spartans’ total offense to under 300 yards. Defensive coordinator Jay Hill often gets his props, but it’s worth remembering just how strong this defense is simply because of the players on the field — and if Michigan is to win in Eugene, it’s going to need another incredible performance from its defense.

Fiction: Michigan’s offense will look reinvigorated

Firing Beck isn’t going to magically make the Wolverines’ offense better. I know most people aren’t claiming that, but I’m also going to claim this Michigan offense is going to take marginal steps, if that, at getting better in the next three weeks.

The interim offensive coordinator and play caller is Jim Harding, an offensive line coach whose position group has regressed since seasons past. Although varying severity, the offensive line also dealt with injuries last year but still ran for 210.2 yards per game compared to 128.7 this season. Point being, Harding has also underperformed as a position coach.

How much Harding’s shortcomings on Saturdays were a result of Beck will remain to be seen, but the Wolverines are still considering playing two different quarterbacks, haven’t found a true running back rotation, haven’t utilized their tight ends at all, and haven’t found a groove on the offensive line. All those problems can’t be solved in a week, and playing in the Pacific Northwest this weekend won’t make things easier.

michigan.headline: Despising Whittingham: Am I being Irrational?
michigan.body:
Despising Whittingham: Am I being Irrational?

I posted this in another thread and saw a lot folks agreeing.  Curious how the rest of the board feels.

I’ve never actually despised a UM head coach.
I’m not part of a “lunatic fringe” and was never for Harbaugh being fired, and even hoped for RR and Hoke to succeed after a horrific start and annual regression, respectively.

I’ve even become less passionate about UM sports as I’ve gotten older, so I am a bit surprised to have this feeling, but I actually have a visceral reaction every time I see Whittingham interviews and am disgusted at any comment or appearance he makes at this point. He feels so distant and disconnected from the program, players and fans - as if he is doing everyone a favor just being in Ann Arbor.

Again, I say this as someone who lived through the frustration of the latter Carr years, RR and Hoke, but never grew to despise the individuals beyond being critical of coaching and performance.
The combination of Whittingham’s arrogance, incompetence, and flippant attitude to the fanbase and media disgusts me. It feels as if he swings between disengaged and and tone deaf to actually having a disdain for the program and its traditions.  It’s one thing for someone to be past his prime (Carr), a bad fit (RR) or in over his head (Hoke), but another for someone to act as sanctimonious and above it all, with dismissive comments on rivalries, trophy games and the players.

Again, I’ve seen bad to terrible football by UM before, but I’ve never had this deep loathing for anyone in charge of or even involved with the program. I can only imagine what the players think of this guy, as I haven’t seen one current player come to his defense. When he talks about his history and what worked at Utah, it feels like a criticism of the current players, not just “be patient” talk.
Am I being nuts here?  Is this just my perception being clouded by bad football, or do others also see him as a disengaged prick?

msu.headline: Getting To Know The Enemy: 6Qs About The Washington Huskies
msu.body:
SEATTLE, WA - OCTOBER 09: Washington head coach Jedd Fisch instructs the official during the college football game between the Washington Huskies and the Iowa Hawkeyes on October 9, 2026, at Husky Stadium in Seattle, WA. (Photo by Jesse Beals/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

Happy Thursday, TOC Nation. Our Michigan State Spartans Football Team is riding high after knocking off um, and is now looking to turn that into some momentum for the final quarter of the season. I sat down with Mark Schafer from UW Dawg Pound to learn about this weekend’s foe, the Washington Huskies. Let’s see what he had to say.

The Only Colors: This is year 3 for Washington in the Big Ten. How are you enjoying life in your new conference? Do you feel like the distance component of many of your games is an issue?
What were your expectations coming into 2026?

Mark Schafer:  While I do like the variety in all of the teams the Huskies face, and I do think it’s interesting to
see how the Huskies slot into the pecking order of the new Big Ten, part of me misses the old regional based conferences. But, right, wrong or otherwise, this is the business we’ve chosen. So I like it from a competition standpoint, but I do miss being in the PAC 12 sometimes. Part of that is the distance component. Before this year, Jedd Fisch’s major pitfall as a coach was his inability to win outside of the Pacific Time Zone. He has surprised some by winning both conference road games outside of the Pacific Time Zone (at Purdue and at Nebraska). However, the team has fallen well short of expectations for this season. Ranked at 17 to start the year, there was talk of a playoff berth with all the talent on offense and defense. However, that talent has yet to translate into many decisive victories, which has been incredibly maddening. In my mind, it comes down to 2 men, the head coach and the starting quarterback.

TOC: Your quarterback is Demond Williams Jr. He got knocked out of the sixth game of the season with an injury, missed a game, got put in late in the following game, and then started your most recent game – a loss to Penn State. Washington did win the 2 games he did not start, though Williams was on the field for the Huskies’ only offensive TD of the latter one. Is he the better QB option? What are his strengths and weaknesses?

MS: For starters, because of his athletic ability, I believe that he is a better option over Elijah Brown (who gets the ball out faster but doesn’t have the best arm). But don’t mistake this for him being head and shoulders above the competition. He has regressed in terms of his decision making from a pretty good 2025 season. It seems like he holds onto the ball too long and doesn’t know what to do when you pressure him, which results in him sailing throws, overshooting on deep shots, and missing receivers when he should be hitting them in stride. It also seems like he’s trying too hard to make a big play and he forces it when it’s not there. But it’s also part of the Demond Williams experience, because when he does make the big play, it gives the Huskies the shot of momentum they often need to sustain drives. Most of the time, it’s frustrating, but when he gets going and takes what’s there, he can be a pretty good quarterback. The issue is the consistency is not where it should be in year 3.

TOC: Who are the skill position players on Washington that MSU fans should worry about?

MS: The wide receivers are particular standouts. Due to the rash of injuries to the running backs, both
Chris Lawson (the Huskies’ leading receiver with 48 catches, 727 yards and 3 touchdowns) and
Dezmen Roebuck (who leads the team in receiving touchdowns with 4) have seen occasional
time in the backfield. They are great receivers with incredible athletic ability, and Lawson
especially has been a particularly surprising breakout. At tight end, the 270 pound Baron Naone
serves as Demond Williams’ primary safety valve. With 21 catches, 275 yards receiving and 3
touchdowns, the big guy has shown supreme athletic ability for his size, and emerged as an
unexpected TE1 (a role Husky fans expected would go to Decker Degraaf).

In the backfield, it’s been a struggle, as the committee of Trey Cooley (a 6th year senior) and Brian Bonner (a true
Freshman 4 star) have shouldered the load to frustrating results, though Bonner has shown
flashes that suggest he could be a star. I blame that on injuries, as season opening RB1 Quaid
Carr and Jayden Limar have been sidelined for much of the season, but Limar came back for the
Nebraska game and had a team high 66 yards against Penn State. But thanks to said injuries, this
team is pass first, second, and third.

TOC: What is the base formation of the Huskies’ defense? Which level of the defense is its best? Who is the one name on this side of the ball that the MSU coaching staff must scheme for?

MS: DC Ryan Walters runs a base 4-2-5 defense, but uses a lot of exotic looks to disguise what he actually is going to try to do, often sending defenders on late blitzes for instance. In terms of personnel, I’d say that the secondary is the best unit of the defense. With talent like safety Rylon Dillard Allen (43 tackles, 2 pass breakups, 3 picks), nickel Dylan Robinson (37 tackles, 4 pass deflections, 1 interception), freshman cornerback Jeron Jones (22 tackles, 3 pass deflections, 2 interceptions), and Emmanuel Karnley (who leads the team is pass deflections with 11), that group has been by far the best on the defensive side of the ball. But the best player on defense is Alex McLaughlin. McLaughlin is a high motor guy who is in on seemingly every play, leading the team in tackles (with 63) and interception return yards (52), and who also has 3 defensive touchdowns in his 2 years at UW. It’s tough to scheme for him because he has great instincts, and hits hard lining up everywhere on the field.

TOC: Fill in the blank: Washington will win if ___. Washington will lose if ___.

MS: UW will win if they can keep Demond Williams comfortable and allow him to get the ball to his
receivers in space where they can make plays (which in my opinion is where he excels the most).
It also won’t hurt to get the running game going if they can, even if that means doing so with
screens or receivers in the backfield.  Any extra option to get yards without relying on one guy is
always good. Defensively, it really comes down to keeping everything in front of them, and
doing that early is key because I, and most other fans, do not prefer wild comebacks and swings
in momentum like last week. If the defense plays like they did in the first half last week (a
distinct possibility), and the offense continues its slide into something worse than mediocrity,
they will lose.

TOC: Predict the final score.

MS: I predict a low scoring first quarter, Michigan State to slightly pull away and for the Huskies to be down at half, before a few momentum swinging plays allow the Huskies to pull out the victory.
Washington-17, Michigan State-14

TOC: Bonus question: Aside from former athletes, who is Washington’s most famous alum?

MS: UW has plenty of non-athlete alums who are notable. Frank Herbert (author of Dune) went to UW, as did Beverly Cleary (author of the Ramona Quimby series of children’s books), smooth jazz saxophonist Kenny G, Ken Jennings (owner of a 74 day winning streak on Jeopardy!, and now the show’s host), Rainn Wilson (known for playing the role of Dwight Schrute on The Office), and the late great Bruce Lee. Joel McHale (best known for playing Jeff on Community) is a unique case, as he was actually a walk on tight end for 2 seasons, though he did not play in any games.

msu.headline: Spartans Host Washington; Look to Build Off UM Win
msu.body:
SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 07: Demond Williams Jr. #1 of the Washington Huskies passes against the Penn State Nittany Lions during the first half at Husky Stadium on November 07, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Hard to believe we are now in the last quarter of the 2026 football regular season and the Spartans have just two more games in Spartan Stadium.  The first is this Saturday against the Washington Huskies (4:15 PM ET, BTN).  Here, we’ll take a closer look at the Huskies and some of the storylines for this game.

Join the conversation!

Fewer ads

Washington Season Recap

Washington enters at 5-4 overall and 2-4 in the Big Ten.  The Huskies are coming off a 28-25 home loss to Penn State.

UW didn’t play the toughest non-conference schedule in facing Washington State, Utah State, and Eastern Washington and emerged 3-0 to start the season.  The Big Ten hasn’t been as kind but one thing that might be in the Huskies’ favor is that their two conference wins have come on the road – against Purdue (October 16) and Nebraska (October 31).

In addition to Penn State, Washington has lost at USC and dropped home games to Minnesota and Iowa.

Most of the Huskies’ games have been close.  The largest margin of victory in conference was against Purdue (38-26) and biggest defeat was to Iowa (41-24).  Washington’s other conference games were all within one score.

Washington Offense

Demond Williams Jr. is Washington’s quarterback and, like Washington’s season, his play has been up and down.  Williams is a 5-11, 190 lb junior who saw action for the Huskies as a true freshman, where he completed 78% of his passes for 844 yards, eight touchdowns and one interception.  Williams became Washington’s full-time starter as a sophomore last year, completing nearly 70% of his passes for 3065 yards and 25 TDs.

This performance reportedly led to a big NIL deal to keep Williams at Washington but outside influences apparently still managed to find a way to . . . influence.  Williams announced his intention to enter the transfer portal on January 6 but Washington, citing his NIL contract, refused to enter his name.  Two days later, Williams announced his intention to stay at UW.

It was a short-lived distraction but one has to wonder if this has had any impact on Washington’s team dynamics and season so far.  The Huskies went 9-4 last year, with a bowl win over Boise State, as Williams put together a great season.  Washington will need to win out just to match that record this year.

Williams is also not producing at quite the same level. His completion percentage has dropped to 64.5% and his yards per attempt has gone from 8.7 last year to 7.6 this year. In conference play, Williams threw for 239 yards in the loss to Minnesota but didn’t crack 200 in the losses to USC and Penn State. Washington is 0-4 in conference games that Williams has started this year.

Even worse for Williams, he was knocked out of the Iowa game with an injury on October 9 and relieved by junior Elijah Brown.  The Stanford transfer threw for 251 yards against the Hawkeyes and then followed that up 302 more in the Huskies’ win at Purdue.  Brown also led the offense in the win over Nebraska but Washington returned to Williams under center against Penn State.

Bottom line for Michigan State: the Spartans will probably have to prepare for two UW quarterbacks this week.

Neither Washington quarterback has had much help from the run game.  Washington is second-to-last in the Big Ten with only 99.3 rushing yards per game and averages just 3.6 yards per carry.  Michigan State is one spot ahead of UW, averaging 110.1 yards.  The Huskies have had just one game this year with a 100-yard rusher (the win at Purdue).  Freshman Brian Bonner Jr. is UW’s leading rusher with 318 yards on 4.4 ypc and one touchdown.  The quarterback, Williams, is next with 254 yards on 3.5 ypc and two TDs.

Perhaps as a result of the struggling run game, Washington has leaned more heavily on the pass.  The Huskies have thrown the ball on 56% of their offensive plays this year and Williams and Brown have multiple reliable targets.  Five wide receivers and two tight ends have at least 9 catches so far this year but UW does not seem to throw it to their running backs nearly as often.

Washington Defense

The Husky defense has been solid and ranks near the middle of the conference in points allowed per game (10th at 21.9) but teams have been able to move the ball on Washington.  UW is just 13th in the league in giving up 350.4 yards per game (136 rushing and 214.4 passing).  For comparison, the Spartan D now ranks 10th in the league after the great performance against Michigan, in allowing 337 yards per game.

Ryan Walters is Washington’s defensive coordinator and he has been employing the same scheme as when he was DC at Illinois and head coach at Purdue.  The Huskies play a 4-2-5 base but often modify this by bringing a fifth player to the line of scrimmage.  Here’s guessing Walters will do this often against MSU, and possibly stack the box with even more defensive players, in an attempt to get Alessio Milivojevic to put the ball in the air.

Michigan State, however, is unlikely to give up on the run easily.  The Spartans are the opposite of Washington in running on 56% of their offensive plays and MSU found some success on the ground against Michigan’s strong defense.

Middle linebacker Jacob Manu (5-10, 225, SR) organizes Washington’s defense and has 49 tackles and three sacks this year.

What to Watch

Spartans get back to work. Through six straight losses and multiple injuries, this team didn’t quit. That effort finally paid off with a win at Michigan. Now, how well will MSU be able to refocus and get back to work after an emotional win against their rival? After creating great plans for the Michigan game, and having the players execute those plans, what will MSU coordinators Nick Sheridan and Joe Rossi come up with for Washington?

Spartan Stadium advantage.  I feel like I bring this up for every home game but what will the home crowd be like on Saturday?  Pat Fitzgerald has praised the MSU fans all season and said in his post game presser at Michigan that he’s looking for more great support from the Spartan faithful in the last two home games.  As of this writing, it looks like it will be cool (mid-30’s) during the game, but dry.  We’ll see how much excitement the Michigan win generated.  Hopefully the team, and the fans, return to Spartan Stadium ready to go.

Feels like another close one.  As mentioned above, most of Washington’s games have been close this year.  The Spartans did some good things offensively at Michigan but probably aren’t going to light up the scoreboard against Washington.  Washington’s offense probably has a bit more punch than Michigan’s but relies heavily on the pass.  Can the Spartans coverage hold up and can they get pressure on the Husky QB like they did at Michigan?

Go Green!

msu.headline: Michigan State Film Room: Growing Up at the Big House
msu.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 07: Ben Roberts #52 of the Michigan State Spartans celebrates with the Paul Bunyan Trophy after a 15-6 win over the Michigan Wolverines at Michigan Stadium on November 07, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

I’ve been smiling all week. I still can’t quite believe Michigan State went into Ann Arbor and beat michigan. What a feeling. After everything we’ve endured this season, this one feels especially sweet. It’s amazing how sports can make you feel so miserable after a loss, only to turn around and deliver this kind of absolute jubilation. For as bad as I’ve felt watching this team at times, beating that team in their own stadium feels so damn good. God, I love sports.

For much of this season, Michigan State has been a team searching for consistency. We’ve spent plenty of time in the Film Room examining missed assignments, costly penalties and opportunities that slipped away. There have been flashes of what this team could become, but rarely have the Spartans put together a complete performance. Against michigan, we finally got to see what happens when those pieces come together. And what better place to do it than the Big House?

Michigan State’s 15-6 victory wasn’t necessarily pretty, particularly on offense, but the scoreboard doesn’t tell the whole story. The Spartans played physical football, controlled possession and showed a level of composure that has too often been missing this season. Meanwhile, michigan appears to have discovered a new rock bottom, somewhere beneath the Brady Hoke and Rich Rodriguez years. The cherry on top? It was Michigan State that helped bring about its downfall, perhaps delivering the final nail in the coffin for the offensive coordinator and maybe even Sleepy Whitt himself. Personally, I’d welcome Whittingham sticking around. This looks like a michigan team the Spartans could enjoy beating year after year.

I asked Robbie this on the Red Cedar Rundown podcast, and I’ll ask it here as well. If Michigan State got to play michigan every week in the Big Ten, wouldn’t the Spartans be in the College Football Playoff conversation by now? Who knew michigan would turn out to be the antidote to all our problems?

There were plenty of individual performances worth highlighting, but three things stood out during my review of the film: an exhausting third-quarter drive, the toughness of Brandon Tullis and a defensive front that made life miserable for michigan quarterback Tommy Carr.

This week’s Film Room is a little longer than usual, but after watching Michigan State dismantle michigan in Ann Arbor, there was simply too much good football to leave on the cutting room floor.

Let’s head into the Film Room.

The Drive That Broke michigan

Sometimes the most important possession of a football game doesn’t end with a touchdown. Michigan State’s third-quarter drive was a perfect example. After forcing michigan to punt on its opening possession of the second half, the Spartans found themselves backed up at their own 1-yard line. What followed was a 17-play, 79-yard drive that consumed 10 minutes, 41 seconds and ended with a field goal by Liam Boyd (No. 37).

It wasn’t a highlight reel of explosive plays. Instead, it was a collection of tough runs, timely completions and crucial third-down conversions. Brandon Tullis (No. 7) and Kenneth Williams (No. 32) provided the physical running presence, while Alessio Milivojevic (No. 11) made the throws necessary to keep the chains moving. No single play defined the drive. It was Michigan State’s ability to consistently move the chains that made it so impressive.

One of the biggest plays came on 3rd-and-6, when Williams took a draw up the middle, made a sharp jump cut and broke into the open field for a crucial conversion. Tullis followed with another physical run, fighting through multiple defenders for additional yardage. Later in the drive, a short pass to Samson Gash (No. 5) helped keep michigan’s defense guessing. The wolverines couldn’t get off the field, couldn’t generate momentum and could only watch as the Spartans continued draining the clock.

There is certainly room for criticism. Michigan State became conservative as the field shortened, and the drive ultimately produced only three points. I’d have liked to see offensive coordinator Nick Sheridan take advantage of michigan’s aggressive pursuit with a play-action pass near the red zone, perhaps looking for Fredrick Moore. Still, the Spartans showed the patience and execution necessary to sustain a possession, even when the defense knew what was coming.

It’s also worth considering what this drive could mean beyond Saturday’s victory. Years from now, we might look back at those 10 minutes, 41 seconds as one of the defining moments of the Pat Fitzgerald era at Michigan State. Perhaps it becomes the drive that changed the trajectory of the season, the possession where Milivojevic established himself as the quarterback capable of leading this program forward, or the moment a frustrated fan base and its donors began believing in the direction of Spartan football again.

That’s a lot of significance to place on a single possession, particularly one that ended in a field goal, but sometimes the moments that define a program aren’t obvious until years later.

Brandon Tullis Earns Every Yard

“My coaches kept encouraging me and kept telling me to keep staying on the same path that I was working on. And the opportunity came, and I provided.”

Those words from Brandon Tullis following Michigan State’s victory over michigan tell you a lot about the patience required to wait for an opportunity. Tullis began the season fifth on the running back depth chart and wasn’t even expected to start against michigan. When Kenneth Williams went down with an injury, Tullis answered the call despite having been injured himself during practice earlier in the week.

To put his performance into perspective, Tullis entered the game with just 11 carries for 53 yards across four appearances this season. Against michigan alone, he carried the football 25 times for 86 yards, averaging 3.4 yards per attempt, with a longest run of just 9 yards. Those aren’t numbers that normally jump off the page, but watch the film, and you’ll understand why Tullis earned our River Rat of the Week honors (grittiest player) on Monday’s Red Cedar Rundown podcast.

Tullis was the definition of a gritty football player against michigan. He doesn’t dilly-dally in the backfield. He gets the football, finds his opening and attacks it. Time after time, he took runs that appeared destined for little or no gain and turned them into positive yardage. He showed patience when necessary, but once he committed to a running lane, he wasn’t going to let the first defender bring him down. Sometimes it took three, four or even five wolverines to finish the job. Tullis wasn’t just running through michigan’s defense. He was taking half their defense along for the ride.

PLAY 1: Tullis Moves the Chains

Before the snap, take a look at Alessio Milivojevic’s (No. 11) eyes. He is absolutely locked in!

Facing a crucial 3rd-and-1 in the second quarter, Michigan State lines up in a heavy formation with an extra offensive lineman to the left and a tight end serving as a fullback. michigan knows what’s coming, stacking eight defenders near the line of scrimmage, and gets exactly the penetration it wants.

Brandon Tullis (No. 7) looks dead to rights for a two-yard loss, with defensive tackles Trey Pierce (No. 95) and Enow Etta (No. 17) getting their hands on him. Linebacker Nathaniel Staehling (No. 44) also has a chance to bring him down. But Tullis lowers his center of gravity, keeps those powerful legs churning and fights through four tackle attempts to somehow pick up the first down. His contact balance and lower-body strength are remarkable, especially with defenders trying to drag him backward.

My favorite part might be Pierce’s reaction afterward. Watch him angrily slap his hands together in frustration. He knows he had Tullis stopped in the backfield, but the running back simply refused to go down.

PLAY 2: Tullis Pile Driver

The next example might be my favorite because it captures what we’ve seen from Tullis throughout the game. Time and again, he’s forced to create his own yardage when the blocking gives him little to work with.

On 2nd-and-8, just before the two-minute mark, Michigan State lines up in a condensed formation while michigan crowds the line with five down linemen and two linebackers, expecting the run. The wolverines get excellent penetration, leaving Brandon Tullis (No. 7) with nowhere to go. But Tullis stays patient, lets the defense overrun the play and shrugs off contact near the hole before running right through Lugard Edokpayi Jr. (No. 88).

At one point, four michigan defenders have their hands on Tullis, but those legs just keep churning. The offensive line eventually comes to his rescue, pushing the pile forward. I thought the officials blew the whistle a little early because Tullis was still fighting for yardage. Once again, his lower-body strength and determination turn what could have been a loss into a manageable third down.

On the following snap, Alessio Milivojevic rolls to his right and finds Kenneth Williams for the first down. michigan adds to its frustration with a late-hit penalty, giving the Spartans even more yardage. What looked like another play going nowhere becomes a drive-extending sequence, all because Tullis refused to go down.

And don’t overlook the blocking by Michigan State’s wide receivers throughout this game. Outside of Chrishon McCray, the receivers didn’t necessarily light up the stat sheet, but they blocked their asses off all afternoon. They played with physicality and a mean streak against a respected michigan defense. That willingness to do the dirty work was another example of Michigan State being the tougher team on this day, and it’s something I hope carries over into the final three games.

PLAY 3: Bully Run Blocking

Finally, let’s return to that marathon third-quarter drive. Following Kenneth Williams’ impressive third-down conversion, Tullis takes a 1st-and-10 handoff near midfield and runs directly into the teeth of michigan’s defense. One defender makes contact, then another, but Tullis keeps driving forward as more wolverines join the tackle. It’s the kind of run that might only produce a handful of yards but takes considerably more effort to stop than the box score suggests. By this point, michigan’s defense had already spent much of the quarter on the field, and Tullis was making sure every additional snap came at a physical cost.

This might be my favorite example of Michigan State imposing its will up front. Center Trent Fraley (No. 63) pancakes his defender, right guard Nick Sharpe (No. 52) delivers an excellent block on michigan’s No. 91, and left tackle Rakeem Johnson (No. 55) takes care of No. 93. Left guard Connor Moore (No. 58) gets a great block on linebacker No. 4, while tight end Kai Rios (No. 88) comes across the formation and smashes into John-Henry Daley (No. 90), one of michigan’s best defenders.

For once, Brandon Tullis (No. 7) gets to attack downhill without having to fight off defenders in the backfield. But he still adds his own finishing touch, putting Rod Moore (No. 1) through the wash cycle with a beautiful spin move that leaves the defender grasping at air.

This play perfectly captures Michigan State’s dominance in the trenches and the physicality this team brought to Ann Arbor. The Spartans weren’t just holding their own against a respected michigan defense. They were taking the fight to the wolverines and winning the battle at the line of scrimmage.

It reminded me a little of Ricky White’s breakout performance against michigan in 2020. Not necessarily because of the statistics or style of play, but because an unexpected contributor stepped forward on the biggest stage. Tullis might not have been the most recognizable name entering this rivalry game, but he certainly made himself known.

And after watching him run through michigan’s defense for four quarters, I’m left with one question.

Where has this Brandon Tullis been all season?

Lafaele and the Defensive Front Take Over

Michigan State’s offense deserves credit for controlling the clock, but the defense was the biggest reason the Spartans left Ann Arbor with the Paul Bunyan Trophy. michigan struggled to establish anything resembling a consistent offensive attack, and much of that came from the Spartans’ ability to pressure quarterback Tommy Carr without sacrificing their defensive responsibilities. The defensive line was particularly impressive, using a combination of physicality, speed and well-executed stunts to keep michigan’s offensive line guessing throughout the afternoon.

One player who caught my attention was Anelu Lafaele (No. 11). Earlier in the season, he appeared to be more of a situational pass rusher, someone the Spartans could unleash off the edge in obvious passing situations. Against michigan, however, he showed improved awareness against the run while remaining a disruptive presence in the passing game. It’s been encouraging to watch him develop into a more complete defensive player.

PLAY 4: Lafaele Brings the Heat

I love the defensive call here by Joe Rossi and the incredible athleticism displayed by Lafaele (No. 11). Not many defensive linemen have the speed and agility to execute this kind of stunt. Lafaele initially attacks to his right, drawing the attention of michigan’s left tackle before quickly changing direction and sprinting back inside toward the middle of the offensive line. The ability to make that sharp change of direction while moving at full speed is impressive, and Lafaele finishes the play by getting to Tommy Carr for the sack.

Just as important is the work being done around him. Defensive tackles Mikeshun Beeler (No. 52) and Eli Coenen (No. 96) occupy multiple offensive linemen, creating the space Lafaele needs to attack the interior. Watch michigan left guard Nathan Efobi (No. 55) panic as Lafaele blows right past him. Efobi realizes too late where the pressure is coming from and desperately tries to recover, but Lafaele is already accelerating toward Carr.

Meanwhile, Kenny Soares Jr. (No. 1) is assigned to spy Carr, staying disciplined in the middle of the defensive front and ready to pursue the quarterback if he manages to escape the pressure.

It’s a beautifully designed and executed defensive stunt that showcases both Rossi’s creativity and the athleticism of his players. Rather than relying on one defender to beat his man, Michigan State uses coordinated movement and disciplined assignments to create pressure. Lafaele gets the sack, but this is a terrific example of all 11 defenders working together.

PLAY 5: Mr. Spartan Unleashed

The final example comes late in the fourth quarter, with michigan attempting a two-point conversion. Kenny Soares Jr., wearing that legendary No. 1 jersey, puts an exclamation point on Michigan State’s defensive performance with a sack of Tommy Carr (No. 14).

What makes this play even better is the unselfish work Soares had done throughout the afternoon. Rather than being turned loose to rush the passer, Soares was frequently tasked with spying Carr, hovering around the line of scrimmage and waiting to chase down the quarterback if he attempted to escape the pocket. It’s not the kind of assignment that fills a stat sheet, but it speaks to the discipline and team-first mentality that make Soares such a valuable player.

Defensive coordinator Joe Rossi saved one of his best weapons for the closing moments. When Soares finally got the opportunity to attack, he unleashed an incredible spin move against michigan left guard Evan Link (No. 71). Somehow, Soares maintained his balance while moving at full speed, quickly changed direction as Carr scrambled away and managed to bring the quarterback down with an ankle tackle. The combination of speed, agility and body control was remarkable. Just an incredible football play.

Soares embodies everything that the No. 1 jersey is supposed to represent at Michigan State. A talented player, an unselfish teammate and a leader willing to do whatever his defense needs. Mr. Spartan delivered one final reminder of why he wears that number.

michigan’s Best Offense

I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention one of the more questionable officiating decisions of the afternoon. In the third quarter, Michigan State appeared to have gotten another important third-down stop, only for the officials to review whether the Spartans had too many men on the field.

The strange part was that no flag had been thrown during the play. Instead, the video assist crew reportedly alerted the officials afterward that a Spartan hadn’t completely cleared the field before the snap. Suddenly, a stray foot was enough to give michigan another opportunity.

PLAY 6: A Little Help From the Stripes

I’ve watched a lot of football, and I can’t recall seeing this type of penalty called after the fact. The timing made it even more suspicious. It came on third down, with michigan trailing by multiple scores, just as Michigan State appeared to have gotten off the field. Maybe it was technically the correct call, but it certainly smelled fishy. And somehow, these unusual officiating decisions always seem to benefit the same team in Ann Arbor.

At times, michigan’s best offense appeared to be the referees. Fortunately, Michigan State’s best defense might have been simply letting Tommy Carr throw the football. Between the questionable calls and Carr’s inability to consistently connect with his receivers, it was a strange afternoon in Ann Arbor. Even with a little assistance from the officials, michigan still couldn’t find a way to do much of anything against the Spartans.

What We Learned and What’s Next

After spending much of this season breaking down everything Michigan State has done wrong, it sure feels good to spend a week talking about what this team did right. The Spartans weren’t perfect against michigan, but they played with a level of physicality, discipline and confidence that we’ve been waiting to see. They controlled the football for more than 38 minutes, forced four turnovers and held michigan to just 192 yards of offense. Perhaps most importantly, they didn’t allow mistakes to snowball into the kind of disasters we’ve witnessed far too often this season. When something went wrong, somebody else stepped up and made a play. That’s what good football teams do.

One of my favorite moments wasn’t even a successful play. Early in the game, Alessio Milivojevic delivered a difficult fourth-down throw to Bryson Williams that the receiver couldn’t bring in. Rather than showing frustration, Milivojevic went over and encouraged his teammate. It’s a small moment that probably goes unnoticed by most people watching, but I think it speaks to the kind of leadership this team is beginning to develop. Milivojevic wasn’t spectacular statistically, finishing with 188 passing yards, but he protected the football, made some impressive throws under pressure and helped Michigan State sustain drives that kept michigan’s defense on the field.

Pat Fitzgerald deserves plenty of credit as well. During the broadcast, I noticed a moment when Fitzgerald was actively taking notes on the sideline while michigan’s coaching staff appeared to be searching for answers. Maybe I’m reading too much into a brief television shot, but it captured the difference between these two teams. Michigan State looked prepared and determined to execute its game plan. The Spartans trusted their defense, leaned on their running game and made michigan prove it could beat them. The wolverines never really came close.

Of course, one victory doesn’t erase the frustrations of the previous two months. Michigan State still has plenty of work ahead, particularly on offense. Settling for five field goals isn’t going to win many football games, and the Spartans need to find ways to turn those long possessions into touchdowns. But there’s something to be said for recognizing progress when it’s right in front of you. We’ve spent weeks wondering whether this team was improving, whether Fitzgerald’s message was getting through and whether the pieces were beginning to come together. For one Saturday in Ann Arbor, we finally got some encouraging answers.

Now comes the challenge of building on that performance. With Washington, Oregon and Rutgers remaining on the schedule, Michigan State has an opportunity to finish the season playing its best football. The Spartans have shown they can compete when they execute their assignments, avoid costly mistakes and play with the kind of physicality we saw against michigan. The question is whether they can carry that same approach into the final three games rather than allowing this victory to become an isolated highlight in an otherwise frustrating season.

Michigan State went into the Big House, physically dominated its biggest rival and brought Paul Bunyan home.

And after everything we’ve endured this season, I intend to enjoy every minute of it.

What stood out most to you from Michigan State’s victory over michigan? Was it the marathon third-quarter drive, Brandon Tullis’ toughness or the defensive performance? Let us know in the comments.

If you haven’t checked it out already, here’s our latest game breakdown on The Red Cedar Rundown. We’re live Sundays on YouTube, so come hang out, give us a like and subscribe while you’re there.

You can also find me on X @W00dsyOwl. Thanks for your support!

Go Green!

msu.headline: Liam Boyd’s Leg Defeats um, Earns Player Of The Game Award
msu.body:
Pasadena, - October 24: Safety Devin Vaught #2 of the Michigan State Spartans strips the ball from running back Anthony Woods #6 of the UCLA Bruins in the first half of a NCAA football game at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena on Saturday, October 24, 2026. (Photo by Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images

It took nine games, but we finally have a repeat winner of the Player of the Game Award.  And it is the Spartan who won the award in our opener who gets back to the mountain top.  In a game that had a few worthy nominees, it was the kicking capabilities of Liam Boyd that stood out.

For the second time this year, Boyd hit 5 field goals, like he did in game 1.  This time, however, he did it without a miss.  He went 5/6 against Toledo and also added an extra point in that one.  But in our win over um, he accounted for 100% of the Spartans’ points as we were never able to get into the endzone.

When Boyd won the award for week 1, he earned 56% of the vote.  For the um game, he surpassed that with 58%.

While Boyd earned more than half the votes, the comment section gave shoutouts to some other players.

RI Spartan was backing NiJhay Burt:

I voted Burt and would again if I could. 2nd on team in tackles and his 2 4th quarter TO were massive for MSU.

And mcgowa14 shared his thought process before settling on the same guy:

Felt like Lafaele was everywhere. Credited with 1 TFL, 1 Sack, 1FF, and 1 Hurry. He has been a difference maker the last few games, but Burt played great, Tulis played great, McCray was rock solid. I think Burt gets the nod for 2 direct turnovers vs the 1 for Lafaele.

So Boyd now has won the award twice.  DT Ben Roberts, RB Cam Edwards, LB Jordan Hall, RB Jaziun Patterson, and S Devin Vaught have each won it once.  And there were two games without a winner.

Congrats to Liam Boyd for winning the award again.  And thank you from Spartan Nation for kicking um’s a$$.

Crystal ball time.  Who will earn Player of the Game next week?

I know Spartan Nation is still basking in the glow of last night’s football victory.  Today, we had more teams playing in big games.  Both the Men’s and Women’s Soccer Teams had Big Ten Tournament games today. tigers.headline: Scott Harris isn’t shopping Riley Greene at the GM Meetings
tigers.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 23: Riley Greene #31 of the Detroit Tigers warms up on the field prior to a game against the Washington Nationals at Comerica Park on September 23, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Brandon Sloter/IOS/Getty Images) | Getty Images

On Tuesday, Jon Morosi of FOX Sports reported from the GM Meetings in Las Vegas that a few executives have mentioned Detroit Tigers’ slugger Riley Greene as a possible trade candidate this offseason. The 26-year-old left fielder has two years remaining until free agency and Scott Harris has shown absolutely zero interest in a long-term contract extension. Yet when Morosi asked the question, Harris also downplayed any rumors around Greene, saying only that he’d listen as part of his due diligence, but views Greene as one of the key players to the Tigers plans. Something here doesn’t add up.

Tigers fans will recall that for the majority of the 2025 season, it looked like Riley Greene had reached a new level as one of the premier sluggers in baseball. He then endured a catastropic collapse after the All-Star break that extended through the postseason. Suddenly Greene was in the doghouse. With his speed declining, the talk of Greene’s new level of dominance rapidly pivoted to whether he was physically breaking down, and whether the Tigers should consider dealing him at peak value.

At the time, my argument was that the 2025-2026 offseason was the perfect time to seek a long-term contract extension. After getting humbled by the worst stretch of his career and with three years left to free agency, it was a pretty good time to strike if they were ever going to do it, but for all the same reasons it was easy to see why the Tigers weren’t pursuing an extension. The Tigers said almost nothing about Greene all offseason and made no move to initiate extension talks. Nor was there ever a hint that they were shopping him in trade.

Harris’ comments are just standard stuff, so I don’t think there’s any reason to read into them too much. The issue of whether to extend, trade, or just ride it out with Riley Greene is much better told through his promixity to free agency, declining speed and defensive numbers, and the lack of any hint that the Tigers have pursued an extension. Perhaps they tried already and kept it quiet, but the reason there are executives reportedly speculating about Greene’s trade availability just comes down to the facts of his performance and team control.

Greene bounced back at the plate in 2026, shaking off his tough August-October of 2025 stretch. He was a huge force at the plate once again, posting a whopping. 370 on-base percentage with 21 homers and a .194 isolated power mark (ISO) on the year. However, concerns about his declining athleticism only got louder as Greene’s defensive numbers collapsed.

Greene was a net -11 in defensive runs saved (DRS) in 2026, and his -5 outs above average (OAA) was the first time in the negative in his career. His 26.6 ft/sec spring speed per Statcast was awful, putting him in below average territory for the second straight season. Other than Gleyber Torres, Spencer Torkelson, and Eduardo Valencia, Greene was the slowest player on the team. He can’t outrun the Tigers’ starting catcher. At age 26, the athleticism that allowed him to play a solid center field early in his major league career is gone. What’s left is a more sluggish outfielder with a noodle arm who can still really punish the baseball.

Greene trimmed his strikeouts this year, and continues to boast premium batspeed and power. This is still a very dangerous hitter, but between his struggles in big spots and the collapse of the rest of his game, he’s looking more and more like a player who should be at least a part-time designated hitter going forward.

So, declining to extend Greene is understandable. He may well be a good power hitter for another half decade, but he’s becoming a liability in most other respects. That makes the possibility of a trade more realistic, perhaps. Harris did say that he considers Greene a big part of their lineup, but he also acknowledged that it’s his job to listen to offers. That’s standard fare, but the circumstances themselves are what adds some interest in the idea.

Tigers OF Riley Greene has been mentioned as a trade candidate by industry execs here at the GM meetings.

Here’s the response from Scott Harris when I asked him about the possibility today on @MLBNetwork. pic.twitter.com/6EFbILePel
— Jon Morosi (@jonmorosi) November 11, 2026

Maybe finding a good offer for Greene just isn’t in the cards. Even at just 26 years old, and despite some signs that he may have another level yet to unlock as an all around hitter, teams are only going to pay so much in prospects for a player who is at least a minor liability in left field and is declining in speed.

For now, the move is to keep Greene unless somehow aggressively pursues a trade, and instead try to help him rebuild some speed in his offseason conditioning. That didn’t happen last season, but then it hadn’t really affected his defense too much at that point. Greene has always thrived as an outfielder by getting good jumps and closing well on the ball to make every catch possible. He was never fast. With those defensive numbers collapsing this year, perhaps he’ll be more motivated to find solutions. His potential value as a free agent two years from now is tracking a lot worse than would’ve been predicted even a year ago. If Greene can turn it around defensively to a degree, the Tigers might find more aggressive suitors for his services at the deadline next summer or next offseason. They might also be more apt to offer an extension offer were that to occur, but he’ll have free agency in his sights by then.

Riley Greene remains a dangerous hitter and one of the more consistent power producers in the game over the last few seasons, but the rest of his game is in shambles. Without any hint of extension talks, we have to assume that Greene is going to reach free agency, and that probably means he’s more available to reasonable trade offers than Scott Harris would like to admit. There’s no reason to diminish your own player by criticizing him publicly or by shopping him aggressively. Harris will do none of those things, but if there’s going to be a surprise trade of any magnitude this offseason, Greene does feel like the likeliest candidate. It’s just hard to picture many teams offering enough for the Tigers to bother right now.

tigers.headline: Tigers to sign RHP Emilio Pagan to a one-year deal, per report
tigers.body:
CINCINNATI, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 02: Emilio Pagan #15 of the Cincinnati Reds throws a pitch during the 7-3 win against the San Diego Padres at Great American Ball Park on September 02, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images

After midnight on Tuesday, Jon Heyman reported that the Detroit Tigers have agreed to a one-year contract worth $11.5 million with veteran closer Emilio Pagán. The 35-year-old has been with the Cincinnati Reds for the last three seasons, but declined a $10 million player option to come to Detroit instead for an extra million and a half. That assumes there are no potential bonuses available. We’ll wait for the full details to emerge and the physical to be completed before we’re sure on all the details.

The theory here is reasonably sound. Pagán consistently posts good strikeout and walk numbers, and he has a reputation as a bullpen leader. His one fatal weakness is his vulnerability to home runs. Obviously the Tigers are banking on getting him out of Great American Ballpark in Cincinnati to drive down the home run rates. That’s a  predictable bit of reasoning, but after watching the Tigers high leverage relievers perform well in the overall stats columns in 2026, but blow a ton of games by giving up a homer at the worst possible time, it’s hard to love trying another older veteran reliever with home run issues next year.

Pagán racked up 25 saves in 45 appearances last year for the Reds. He posted a reasonably solid 3.38 ERA with a 4.18 FIP. His 25.9 percent strikeout rate is pretty good, and we like his low 6.3 percent walk rate. The fly in the ointment is a home run rate of 1.48 per nine innings.

The profile here is extremely fly ball heavy. He had a 59.3 fly ball rate in 2026. If he can keep the ball in the park a little more the Tigers outfield will collect a ton of routine outs, but it’s certainly a very volatile profile. His HR/9 for each of the last three seasons is 1.42, 1.31, and 1.48 in 2026. Pagán has always had home run problems everywhere he’s been, including San Diego, Tampa Bay, Minnesota, Oakland, and Seattle earlier in his career. It’s not just a Great American Ballpark issue. Here’s hoping the Tigers are right about Comerica suppressing home runs much more than the Reds fairly notorious ballpark. Since the fences were moved in, the Tigers home park has played much more neutral to home runs, and not much different than Great American.

Pagán relies heavily on his fourseam fastball, throwing it 62.8 percent of the time in 2026. He has a cutter and a splitter and uses them equally, deploying the splitter mainly to deal with lefties. He generally keeps balanced splits with those two secondary offerings, and that flexibility appeals to the Tigers and was one of the features Scott Harris mentioned looking for at the GM Meetings on Tuesday.

Pagán has plus extension, which helps as the fastball averaged 94.9 mph last year, down a tick from 2025. It does have some hop to it however, averaging 18 inches of induced vertical break. His whiff rates are generally average across the three pitches, but he does manage to minimize hard contact. It’s just that when the hard contact arrives, it tends to leave the park. He helps himself there by posting better than average walk rates, at least.

This is a perfectly fine acquisition, but it feels very Kenley Jansen 2.0 to be honest. Pagán is a little younger at 35, so we’ll hope the little downtick in velocity last season was just a blip. He also is much better than Jansen at locating the zone even when not at his best, so at least walks shouldn’t be an issue. Pagán is only a part-time closer as well, so the Tigers won’t be guaranteeing him save chances, which helps in terms of flexibility. This is a perfectly solid acquisition that should make the pen better, but comes with that later career risk that Pagán might tip into steep decline. If the Tigers go add a better reliever elsewhere, we’ll be thrilled. If not, we’ll cross our fingers again and hope for the best in terms of home runs allowed in unfortunate moments.

tigers.headline: RHP Evan Phillips is a prime relief target for the Tigers in free agency
tigers.body:
LOS ANGELES, CA - OCTOBER 03: Evan Phillips #59 of the Los Angeles Dodgers pitches during Game One of the National League Division Series presented by Booking.com between the Atlanta Braves and the Los Angeles Dodgers at UNIQLO Field at Dodger Stadium on Saturday, October 3, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Daniel Shirey/MLB Photos via Getty Images) | MLB Photos via Getty Images

To no one’s surprise, Scott Harris identified high leverage relief help as his primary focus this offseason during interviews with the media at the GM Meetings in Las Vegas on Tuesday. This was always going to be a priority for a Tigers club that woefully underperformed in 2026, largely due to the bullpen’s performance in high leverage situations holding leads or ties in the late innings. The simplest way to improve the situation is to go out and add a really good reliever who generates a lot of whiffs. Longtime Dodgers reliever Evan Phillips may fit the bill perfectly.

The 32-year-old Phillips is a free agent for the first time this season. He was the 17th round pick of the Atlanta Braves back in 2015, and broke into the big leagues with them in 2018. Phillips was traded that year to Baltimore, and spent the next few years bouncing back and forth between the minor and major leagues. He struck out a ton of hitters, but his control was still a work in progress and the walks got him returned to Triple-A again and again. After a brief stop as a waiver claim with the Tampa Bay Rays, he was DFA’d again and claimed by the Dodgers in 2021. For the next three seasons he was one of the better setup men in the game as the Dodgers got him throwing strikes with a lot more consistency.

In June of 2025, Phillips blew out his UCL and didn’t return to action until July of 2026. When he got back on the mound, his velocity returned to peak form and he was throwing plenty of strikes. He was bit by too many home runs, but the strikeout and walk rates were outstanding. Phillips is a prime target for me this offseason, but he’ll be aggressively pursued as teams love a stuff guy who returns from Tommy John looking strong.

The 31.1 percent K-rate and 5.7 percent BB-rate stand out as the primary appeal here, but the stuff under the hood is really good to back up the numbers. Phillips will mix in a cutter or sinker here and there, but he’s primarily a fourseam-sweeper pitcher. He averaged 96.9 mph on the fourseamer in 2026 with a very good 26.3 percent whiff rate. The pitch has pretty pedestrian movement, but the velocity and command help it to play up. His 86.2 mph sweeper racked up a 34.3 percent whiff rate and remains an outstanding weapon. Hitters batted .059 against it in 2026, and while it will get smacked if he hangs one occasionally, that was a rare occurrence in 2026 and even more rare from 2023-2025.

The one problem appears somewhat glaring but was really more of a fluke. Phillips has never had notable home run trouble, but his 1.73 HR/9 mark this season is a bit grizzly. This doesn’t bother me. He’s never had home run trouble before, and the stuff was better after the surgery than in the two years prior. He only threw 26 innings, and he gave up five homers. Four of them came in a two week span in July right as he returned, and he only allowed one more home run from late July until the end of the season. This is a very small sample of work and shouldn’t be an issue next year.

Ben Clemens at FanGraphs estimates Phillips will get two years, $20 million total on a free agent deal. I tend to think the number will be a little higher than that, but he’s worth it. Add Phillips to a group including Drew Sommers, Will Vest, and one of the Tigers current starters, and you have a pretty strong backend of a bullpen.

tigers.headline: Scott Harris says he’s focused on adding relievers with swing and miss
tigers.body:
Detroit Tigers pitcher Will Vest practices during spring training at TigerTown in Lakeland, Fla. on Thursday, Feb. 12, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The GM Meetings got underway on Monday in Las Vegas. While not typically a source of major news like signings and trades, the looming CBA negotiations and lockout set to begin on December 1 are putting a little different spin on the annual meet-and-greet as teams look to position themselves for the uncertainty to come. For the most part though, this is still an event that produces quotes more than action. Tigers’ president of baseball operations Scott Harris was asked about the club’s offseason focus and said that they’re prioritizing high leverage relief help that adds swing and miss to the bullpen.

The Tigers really have two possible paths to improving a bullpen that was a disaster in high leverage situations in 2026, despite pretty solid numbers overall. Harris talked a lot in his end of the season press conference about building up a big enough surplus in starting pitching that they’ll have good arms spilling over into relief work. As a result of those quotes, we’ve kept in mind that part of the solution for the Tigers might be to go after starting pitching to allow them to use some of their current starters who aren’t really built up to a major league workload to flex into the bullpen instead.

Of course, Harris was very vague about the timetable for such a surplus emerging, and that’s more of a long term perspective. The Tigers have a good crop of young pitchers brewing in the A-ball levels, but few if any of them are at a point where they could be converted and promoted the major leagues next season.

The other path is obviously to target free agent relievers or to try and trade for them. We’re keeping an open mind, as perhaps the final answer will be help from both pathways.

The quote from Harris comes courtesy of Cody Stavenhagen of The Athletic.

“Pitching is going to be the focus for us this winter….We want to add more swing and miss to the back end of our pen. We want to add a stable veteran presence who can get righties out and lefties out and add a little bit more leadership to our clubhouse.“

While Tigers fans can rip him for being a step behind, Harris did try to add more swing and miss last year by bringing in Kenley Jansen and signing Drew Anderson. The duo did strike out a solid amount of hitters, but they failed in the big moments and Anderson seemed much more steady as a starter. Kyle Finnegan was someone they hoped would be a big factor in this regard, but his first year on a two-year guaranteed deal was even worse than Jansen and Anderson’s work. It’s pretty simple to see what the Tigers need. The problem with Harris, now through four seasons running the Tigers, continues to be execution in developing and ungrading the major league roster.

There’s really nothing to do but take him at his word and think about the criteria he lists. He wants right-handed high leverage help, but it’s important to add relievers who can get out lefties and righties both. He wants swing and miss. And he wants a veteran with some leadership qualities. Few of these qualities are present in RHP Jacob Waguespack, the Tigers lone free agent signing for 2027 so far, and that remains an odd decision that crowds the field of right-handed relievers with more mediocrity, but that deal was at least cheap enough to be jettisoned along the way should the Tigers make an upgrade.

Even so, the Tigers have five spots available for right-handed relievers, assuming Drew Sommers, Brant Hurter, and Tyler Holton are all in the pen. Will Vest, Kyle Finnegan, Drew Anderson, Beau Brieske, and Waguespack are already in house, and none of those players have options. We’re not looking too good here in terms of skills, nor in terms of flexibility, folks. Obviously the last two are easily cut, but having zero right-handed relief help with options is a tough starting point.

Based on Harris’ stated desires, we might look to Yankees’ closer David Bednar, who has been a consistent force over the last five years, with only an ugly 2024 campaign for the Pirates marring what has otherwise been an outstanding run for the 32-year-old right-hander. The problem here is that Harris really hates paying top dollar in free agency and that just isn’t compatible with landing good relievers with high strikeout rates. Something is going to have to give, or it will be the Tigers bullpen giving again in 2027.

Bednar is really good, but he’s not Mason Milller or Adrian Morejon either. Even so, Bednar is expected to receive a three-year deal worth around $45M. He also received a qualifying offer from the Yankees, meaning the Tigers would have to surrender their third most valuable draft pick if they signed him. Next year, that pick will be the Competitive Balance Round A selection, expected to be the 43rd overall pick. That’s a pretty valuable pick.

Even when we consider that free agency might look different after the CBA is agreed, giving up that pick while also handing out a fairly pricey contract to a reliever entering his mid-30’s doesn’t feel like a Scott Harris thing to do. Almost certainly, their long term plans center around crushing a draft where they’ll have at worst a top 11 pick in the first round, and possibly as high as the first overall pick if they get extremely lucky in the draft lottery, plus two more picks before the second round and a huge bonus pool.

Harris surprised us with the late signing of Framber Valdez last offseason, by a huge margin the largest free agent deal he’s signed a player to, but that was in response to losing Reese Olson for the season. The need for a killer reliever is great, and I expect Harris to be a little more aggressive in pursuing relief help than usual, but I highly doubt giving up a draft pick is in the plans.

So, that leaves us looking at options like RHP Bryan Abreu and RHP Evan Phillips—I’m pretty intrigued with Phillips in particular—with perhaps someone like 37-year-old RHP Raisel Iglesias as another option. Iglesias doesn’t get quite the strikeout rates as the other two, but his changeup allows him to handle both-handed hitters pretty consistently and he has tons of closing experience. Give me Phillips and I’d be happy.

The fear here would be Harris going bargain bin and landing on RHP Emilio Pagan instead. Pagan doesn’t provide the level of swing and miss that Bednar, Abreu, and Phillips do, but would perhaps thrive in a more neutral ballpark as home runs have been his biggest issue in recent years. The problem is that he’ll be 36, saw his velocity dip a bit this year, and has given up a lot of homers everywhere he’s gone his whole career. If they’re not actually so caught up in swing and miss, a big-time strike thrower and ground ball getter like RHP Jonathan Loásiga might be a better option in my opinion over Pagan. Neither should be too expensive, and that might allow the Tigers to continue to pursue a top relief arm.

Of course, there’s also the trade market, but as Harris has rarely made a notable trade that didn’t involve the Tigers selling off assets whose team control was coming to an end, it’s pretty hard to see a big trade for a reliever happening. Mason Miller might be on the block for offers, but would probably cost Max Clark and a quality pitching prospect or something like Bryce Rainer and Cameron Flukey. That’s not Harris-ball.

Looking to top relievers who reach free agency in 2028, whose teams might decide to cash them in before the lockout, the top possibilities would be the Brewers closer, Trevor Megill, or Phillies closer Jhoan Duran. Both would cost a lot, and there’s nothing to suggest either team is interested in trading their ace relievers just yet. Seranthony Dominguez might be obtainable from the Mariners, and he continues to post good strikeout rates, but he’s also coming off a pretty bad year. Still, that does feel like a Harris move, hoping to land the veteran reliever cheap and get more out of him than the Mariners did this year.

Harris noted on Tuesday that Tigers’ closer Will Vest is doing very well in recovering from elbow and hip surgeries, and that they expect him to be ready to go next year. That would certainly help the cause if Vest can get back to his 2024-2025 prime form, but no one wants to depend on that either. Even so, with Drew Sommers emerging as one of the nastier southpaw relievers in the game, the Tigers aren’t really so far from putting together a much better bullpen. Getting one good caliber right-handed reliever and adding some starting depth to allow them to use River Ryan, Keider Montero, or potentially Reese Olson in the pen as well, would put them in much better position to contend in 2027.

Scott Harris today: "Pitching is going to be the focus for us this winter. … We want to add more swing and miss to the back end of our pen. We want to add a stable veteran presence who can get righties out and lefties out and add a little bit more leadership to our clubhouse."
